INPUT DATA: {"lesson":{"id":"orbitals","label":"Atomic orbitals and quantum numbers","title":"Atomic orbitals and quantum numbers","molecule":"ethene","tag":"Orbitals describe probability, not paths","cards":{"rule":"

n = 1,2,… sets the shell. l = 0,…,n−1 sets the subshell (s,p,d,f). mₗ = −l,…,+l labels orbitals; mₛ = ±1/2 labels electron spin. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

In the usual multielectron-atom model, subshell energies within one shell increase s < p < d < f (for subshells allowed in that shell). In the nonrelativistic hydrogen-like model, orbitals with the same n have equal energy; do not apply the multielectron splitting to that model.

","cue":"

One s orbital; three p orbitals; five d orbitals; seven f orbitals. A p subshell can hold six electrons. For hydrogen-like atomic orbitals: total nodes = n−1; angular nodes = l; radial nodes = n−l−1. A 3p orbital has one angular node and one radial node.

","trap":"

Orbital phase signs are wavefunction signs, not positive and negative electric charges. Electrons do not orbit like planets. s orbitals have spherical angular symmetry; a p orbital has two lobes separated by a nodal plane. Higher-n orbitals may also have radial nodes. A node is a zero of the wavefunction, not a place where an electron waits.

","app":"

Carbon bonding uses valence orbitals from the second shell. Hybridization is a model for bonding and geometry, not a change in the allowed quantum numbers.

"},"steps":[{"label":"1. Count valence electrons","text":"

The molecular drawing is ethene, H₂C=CH₂, shown as a later bonding example. The separate box diagram describes an isolated neutral carbon atom: 1s²2s²2p², with four valence electrons in the n=2 shell. Do not interpret the C=C lines as orbital boxes or apply the isolated-atom occupancy directly to a bonded carbon.

","molecule":"ethene","highlights":{"prin":[0]},"reveal":true,"diagram":{"type":"orbitals","caption":"Isolated neutral carbon, ground-state filling: 1s² 2s² 2p². This atomic model is distinct from the ethene bonding example.","subshells":[{"label":"1s","electrons":[2]},{"label":"2s","electrons":[2]},{"label":"2p","electrons":[1,1,0]}]}},{"label":"2. Fill degenerate orbitals","text":"

In the isolated-carbon box diagram, the two 2p electrons occupy separate degenerate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund’s rule). Electrons paired in a single orbital have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion). Ethene is the molecular example above; its bonding orbitals are a different model, developed in the next lesson.

","molecule":"ethene","highlights":{"prin":[0,1]},"reveal":true,"diagram":{"type":"orbitals","caption":"Isolated neutral carbon, ground-state filling: 1s² 2s² 2p². INPUT DATA: {"lesson":{"id":"sigma-pi","label":"Sigma, pi, and molecular orbitals","title":"Sigma, pi, and molecular orbitals","molecule":"ethene","tag":"End-on vs. side-on overlap","cards":{"rule":"

A sigma bond has electron density along the internuclear axis. A pi bond comes from side-on p-orbital overlap. A double bond has one sigma and one pi; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi. Constructive overlap forms a lower-energy bonding MO; destructive overlap gives an antibonding MO with an added node.

For comparable carbon–carbon bonds, an individual pi contribution is generally weaker than the sigma contribution because side-on overlap is less effective. Nevertheless, a double bond and a triple bond are generally stronger and shorter overall than a single bond. Their strength increments are unequal; do not add universal, context-free sigma and pi energies.

","cue":"

Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)/2 in the simple MO model. More bond order usually means shorter, stronger bonds for a given atom pair.

","trap":"

A pi bond restricts rotation because twisting disrupts overlap. Bond rotation is possible only by paying an energy cost; do not imagine a double bond freely rotating at room temperature.

","app":"

Carbonyl addition converts a pi bond into sigma bonds. Following sigma and pi electrons helps explain the change from planar to tetrahedral geometry.

"},"steps":[{"label":"1. Double bond inventory","text":"

Ethene has one C–C sigma bond, one C–C pi bond, and four C–H sigma bonds: five sigma and one pi overall. The H₂C and CH₂ labels show the hydrogens; the four C–H bonds are not drawn as separate lines.

","cue":"

For ordinary carbon: four electron domains → sp³; three → sp²; two → sp. A multiple bond counts as one domain.

","trap":"

Do not mechanically label an amide nitrogen sp³ just because it has three sigma bonds and a lone pair. Its lone pair occupies a p orbital conjugated with the carbonyl, making the amide approximately planar.

Peptide-bond resonance restricts C–N rotation. Delocalized charge explains carboxylate stability and why its two C–O bonds are equivalent in the resonance hybrid.
